statement: What is the smallest positive integer $n$ such that every set of $n$ distinct integers chosen from $\{1, 2, \ldots, 50\}$ must contain two different numbers whose product is a perfect square?

choices.misconception: I made one box for each of the 15 primes up to 50 and added 1.
I found the largest set with no square product, which has 31 numbers, and gave its size instead of one more.
I counted the squarefree numbers by removing multiples of 4, 9 and 25 and adding back 36, but forgot that multiples of 49 are not squarefree, so I got 32 boxes.
I thought a product is a perfect square only when both numbers are squares, so I allowed all 43 non-squares plus one square in a safe set.

hints: Write each number as a perfect square times a leftover part.
Two numbers multiply to a perfect square exactly when their squarefree parts are equal. The squarefree parts are the pigeonholes, so count how many there are among 1 to 50.
The possible squarefree parts are exactly the squarefree numbers from 1 to 50. Count them with inclusion-exclusion on the multiples of 4, 9, 25 and 49.

solutions.reliable: Write each number as $s k^2$ with $s$ squarefree. If $a = s k^2$ and $b = t m^2$, then $ab$ is a square exactly when $st$ is a square, which for squarefree $s, t$ means $s = t$. So the numbers fall into classes by squarefree part, and two numbers have a square product exactly when they share a class. The classes correspond to the squarefree numbers up to 50: $50 - (12 + 5 + 2 + 1) + 1 = 31$, where we removed multiples of $4, 9, 25, 49$ and added back $36$. The 31 squarefree numbers themselves form a set with no square product, so $n \ge 32$. Any 32 numbers put two into one of the 31 classes, so $n = 32$. Transferable idea: sort numbers by squarefree part when products must be squares, then use pigeonhole.
